before.title: Periodic Sobolev embedding: H^s on the three-torus controls C^m when s minus m exceeds three halves
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let integers $s\ge m\ge0$ satisfy $s-m>3/2$, and
let $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ with the objects and notation of
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]]. Then:

**(a)** There is a unique representative $u^*\in C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$
of the class $u$, and for every $|\alpha|\le m$ the series
$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ converges absolutely and
uniformly on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ to $D^\alpha u^*$; moreover there is
$C=C(s,m,N)$ with
$$\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\,\|u\|_{H^s}.$$

**(b)** Writing $d(x,y):=\min\{\,|x-y+2\pi l|:l\in\mathbb Z^3\,\}$ for the
induced metric on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and fixing
$0<\theta\le\min\{1,s-m-\tfrac32\}$, there is $C'=C'(s,m,N,\theta)$ with
$$\bigl|D^\alpha u^*(x)-D^\alpha u^*(y)\bigr|\le C'\,\|u\|_{H^s}\,d(x,y)^\theta\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi},\ |\alpha|\le m).$$

**(c)** The assignment $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and if $(u_j)$ is a sequence in
$H^s$ with $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, then $u_j^*\to u^*$ uniformly together with all
derivatives of order at most $m$.

Skipper), Lecture Notes: Navier-Stokes Equations (Universitat Ulm, WS 2018/19), Section 2.1 (Fourier characterisation of the Sobolev spaces H^s(T^3), the continuous embedding H^s(T^3) into L-infinity and the Banach-algebra property for s>3/2) and Section 4.3 (Agmon's inequality)

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on
$[a,b]$. Then there is a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ such
that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. If continuous functions $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ converge uniformly to $f:X\to\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $f$ is continuous.

derivations.claim: (Absolute convergence of the differentiated coefficient series.) Fix $|\alpha|\le m$ and put $\theta_\alpha:=s-|\alpha|\ge s-m>3/2$. For every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$, Cauchy--Schwarz [L4] with $a_k:=|k^\alpha|$ and $b_k:=|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$ gives $\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha|^2(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta_\alpha}\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}(1+|k|^2)^{\theta_\alpha}|\widehat u(k)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; passing to the supremum over finite $F$ by [L3] and using $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}$, and $\theta_\alpha+|\alpha|=s$, yields $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{-(s-m)}\bigr)^{1/2}N_s(u)$.

(The weight sum is finite.) For $\theta>3/2$, $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta}<+\infty$: the ball $|k|\le1$ contributes at most $27$ terms, and the dyadic shell $2^j\le|k|<2^{j+1}$ ($j\ge0$) contains at most $C_3 2^{3j}$ lattice points each weighted by at most $2^{-2j\theta}$, so the shell sum is at most $C_3 2^{-j(2\theta-3)}$ and $\sum_j2^{-j(2\theta-3)}<\infty$ by the geometric series. Hence with $\theta:=s-m$ step 1.1 gives $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le C_{s,m}N_s(u)\le C'_{s,m}\|u\|_{H^s}$ by [L1].

(The limit series gives a $C^m$ representative.) For finite $F$ put $S_F:=\sum_{k\in F}\widehat u(k)\chi_k$, a $C^\infty$ function. If $F,G$ are finite then $\|S_F-S_G\|_{C^m}\le\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sum_{k\in F\triangle G}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$, and the tail sums tend to zero along the finite-subset net by [L3] and step 2.1; hence the derivative series for every $|\alpha|\le m$ satisfies the uniform Cauchy property on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. Applying the interval differentiation theorem [L5] successively along each coordinate direction and for each order gives a $C^m$ function $u^*$ with $D^\alpha u^*=\sum_k(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ for every $|\alpha|\le m$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly by step 2.1; and $\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u\|_{H^s}$ by step 2.1. Since $S_F\to u$ in $L^2$ by [L2] and $S_F\to u^*$ uniformly, $u^*$ represents the class $u$; two continuous representatives of one $L^2$ class agree everywhere, giving uniqueness. This proves (a).

(The Hölder modulus (b).) ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $\mu$, $\chi_k$,
$\widehat u(k)$, the weak derivatives $D^\alpha$ and the spaces
$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be as in
[[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]], and put
$$N_s(u)^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^s\,|\widehat u(k)|^2,\qquad |k|^2:=k_1^2+k_2^2+k_3^2 .$$

**(a)** Let $u\in H^s$ and let $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $|\alpha|\le s$. Then
$D^\alpha u\in H^{s-|\alpha|}$ and
$$\widehat{D^\alpha u}(k)=(ik)^\alpha\,\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3),\qquad (ik)^\alpha:=\prod_{j=1}^3(ik_j)^{\alpha_j}.$$

**(b)** Let $u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ satisfy $N_s(u)<\infty$.
Then $u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$, and there are constants
$0<c_s\le C_s<\infty$, depending only on $s$, such that
$$c_s\,N_s(u)^2\le\|u\|_{H^s}^2\le C_s\,N_s(u)^2 .$$
The right-hand inequality holds for every $u\in H^s$, so the two norms are
equivalent on $H^s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on
$[a,b]$. Then there is a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ such
that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. If continuous functions $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ converge uniformly to $f:X\to\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $f$ is continuous.

[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of compositions
$u\circ q$ of smooth maps $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ that are $2\pi$-periodic
in each variable; these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when
$N=1$). For $m\ge0$ let $C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of
$u\circ q$ with $u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$ $2\pi$-periodic in each
variable ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}\bigl|(D^\alpha u)(x)\bigr| ,$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the multi-index derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] applied to any
periodic representative; the displayed expression is independent of the
representative.

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when their representatives $F(t,q(x),u)=G(t,x,u)$ have
$G\in C^\infty$. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on
$[a,b]$. Then there is a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ such
that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. If continuous functions $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ converge uniformly to $f:X\to\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $f$ is continuous.

before.claim: (Absolute convergence of the differentiated coefficient series.) Fix $|\alpha|\le m$ and put $\theta_\alpha:=s-|\alpha|\ge s-m>3/2$. For every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$, Cauchy--Schwarz [L4] with $a_k:=|k^\alpha|$ and $b_k:=|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$ gives $\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha|^2(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta_\alpha}\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}(1+|k|^2)^{\theta_\alpha}|\widehat u(k)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; passing to the supremum over finite $F$ by [L3] and using $|k^\alpha|^2\le(1+|k|^2)^{|\alpha|}$, and $\theta_\alpha+|\alpha|=s$, yields $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{-(s-m)}\bigr)^{1/2}N_s(u)$.

(The weight sum is finite.) For $\theta>3/2$, $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta}<+\infty$: the ball $|k|\le1$ contributes at most $27$ terms, and the dyadic shell $2^j\le|k|<2^{j+1}$ ($j\ge0$) contains at most $C_3 2^{3j}$ lattice points each weighted by at most $2^{-2j\theta}$, so the shell sum is at most $C_3 2^{-j(2\theta-3)}$ and $\sum_j2^{-j(2\theta-3)}<\infty$ by the geometric series. Hence with $\theta:=s-m$ step 1.1 gives $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le C_{s,m}N_s(u)\le C'_{s,m}\|u\|_{H^s}$ by [L1].

(The limit series gives a $C^m$ representative.) For finite $F$ put $S_F:=\sum_{k\in F}\widehat u(k)\chi_k$, a $C^\infty$ function. If $F,G$ are finite then $\|S_F-S_G\|_{C^m}\le\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sum_{k\in F\triangle G}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$, and the tail sums tend to zero along the finite-subset net by [L3] and step 2.1; hence the derivative series for every $|\alpha|\le m$ satisfies the uniform Cauchy property on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. Applying the interval differentiation theorem [L5] successively along each coordinate direction and for each order gives a $C^m$ function $u^*$ with $D^\alpha u^*=\sum_k(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ for every $|\alpha|\le m$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly by step 2.1; and $\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u\|_{H^s}$ by step 2.1. Since $S_F\to u$ in $L^2$ by [L2] and $S_F\to u^*$ uniformly, $u^*$ represents the class $u$; two continuous representatives of one $L^2$ class agree everywhere, giving uniqueness. This proves (a).

(The Hölder modulus (b).) For $x,y$ and $|\alpha|\le m$, $|D^\alpha u^*(x)-D^\alpha u^*(y)|\le\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\,|\chi_k(x)-\chi_k(y)|\le\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\min\{2,|k|d(x,y)\}$ by [L6]. For $0<\theta\le1$ one has $\min\{2,t\}\le2^{1-\theta}t^\theta$ for every $t\ge0$ (for $t\le2$ because $2^{1-\theta}t^\theta\ge t$ iff $2\ge t$; for $t\ge2$ because $t^\theta\ge2^\theta$), so the sum is at most $2^{1-\theta}d(x,y)^\theta\sum_k|k|^{m+\theta}|\widehat u(k)|\le C_\theta d(x,y)^\theta\|u\|_{H^s}$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1 applied with exponent $s-(m+\theta)>3/2$, valid for $\theta<s-m-3/2$; for the endpoint value $\theta_0=\min\{1,s-m-3/2\}$ choose $\theta<\theta_0$ and use $d(x,y)^{\theta_0}\ge \operatorname{diam}(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi})^{\theta_0-\theta}d(x,y)^\theta$. This proves (b).

(Linearity and convergence (c).) $D^\alpha$ is linear and the series representation is linear in the coefficients, so $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and for $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, applying (a) to the difference gives $\|u_j^*-u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u_j-u\|_{H^s}\to0$, which is uniform convergence of all derivatives of order at most $m$.

after.claim: (Absolute convergence bound.) For $|\alpha|\le m$, finite Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le\bigl(\sum_{k\in F}|k^\alpha|^2(1+|k|^2)^{-s}\bigr)^{1/2}N_s(u)\le\bigl(\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{-(s-m)}\bigr)^{1/2}N_s(u)$. Finite-subset suprema preserve this inequality.

(The weight sum is finite.) For $\theta>3/2$, $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)^{-\theta}<+\infty$: the ball $|k|\le1$ contributes at most $27$ terms, and the dyadic shell $2^j\le|k|<2^{j+1}$ ($j\ge0$) contains at most $C_3 2^{3j}$ lattice points each weighted by at most $2^{-2j\theta}$, so the shell sum is at most $C_3 2^{-j(2\theta-3)}$ and $\sum_j2^{-j(2\theta-3)}<\infty$ by the geometric series. Hence with $\theta:=s-m$ step 1.1 gives $\sum_k|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|\le C_{s,m}N_s(u)\le C'_{s,m}\|u\|_{H^s}$ by [L1].

(The limit series gives a $C^m$ representative.) For finite $F$ put $S_F:=\sum_{k\in F}\widehat u(k)\chi_k$, a $C^\infty$ function. If $F,G$ are finite then $\|S_F-S_G\|_{C^m}\le\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sum_{k\in F\triangle G}|k^\alpha||\widehat u(k)|$, and the tail sums tend to zero along the finite-subset net by [L3] and step 2.1; hence the derivative series for every $|\alpha|\le m$ satisfies the uniform Cauchy property on $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$. Applying the interval differentiation theorem [L5] successively along each coordinate direction and for each order gives a $C^m$ function $u^*$ with $D^\alpha u^*=\sum_k(ik)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\chi_k$ for every $|\alpha|\le m$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly by step 2.1; and $\|u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u\|_{H^s}$ by step 2.1. Since $S_F\to u$ in $L^2$ by [L2] and $S_F\to u^*$ uniformly, $u^*$ represents the class $u$; two continuous representatives of one $L^2$ class agree everywhere, giving uniqueness. This proves (a).

(The Hölder endpoint.) Put $d=d(x,y)$ and $q=s-m$, an integer at least $2$. Cauchy--Schwarz and [L6] bound the square of the derivative difference by $N_s(u)^2 S(d)$, where $S(d)=\sum_k(1+|k|^2)^{-q}\min\{4,|k|^2d^2\}$. For $0<d\le1$ split at $|k|=d^{-1}$. A dyadic shell of radius $L\ge1$ has at most $C L^3$ points. If $q=2$, its low-frequency contribution is at most $C d^2 L$; summing shells up to $d^{-1}$ gives at most $C d$, while high shells contribute at most $C L^{-1}$ and sum to at most $C d$. If $q\ge3$, the entire series $\sum_k |k|^2(1+|k|^2)^{-q}$ converges by the same shell estimate, so $S(d)\le C d^2$. Thus the endpoint exponent is $1/2$ for $q=2$ and $1$ for $q\ge3$, exactly $\min\{1,q-3/2\}$. Smaller positive exponents follow since $d^{\theta_0}\le\max\{1,\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb T^3)^{\theta_0-\theta}\}d^\theta$; for $d>1$ use the sup norm from (a), and for $d=0$ the claim is immediate. This proves (b) with all its stated endpoints.

(Linearity and convergence (c).) $D^\alpha$ is linear and the series representation is linear in the coefficients, so $u\mapsto u^*$ is linear; and for $u_j\to u$ in $H^s$, applying (a) to the difference gives $\|u_j^*-u^*\|_{C^m}\le C\|u_j-u\|_{H^s}\to0$, which is uniform convergence of all derivatives of order at most $m$. [step 3.1, algebra] ∎





- **Sharpness.** The hypothesis $s-m>3/2$ is exactly the case here; The companion counterexample on the examples page shows that for $s-m<3/2$ no continuous representative of all $H^s$ classes need exist, so the boundary is not an artefact of the proof.
- **Use.** The case $m=s-3$ ($s\ge5$) supplies the $L^\infty$ control of all derivatives of order at most $s-3$ used in [[lem-gr-periodic-sobolev-algebra]] and [[lem-gr-smooth-composition-and-commutator-estimates]]; the case $m=s-2$ is used in the time-derivative induction of [[lem-gr-galerkin-time-derivative-bound]], and $m=0$ gives the continuous representative used in the Ascoli step.
